newsitem.title: UK: Czechs, Poles seen exporting sugar from surpluses.
newsitem.headline: Czechs, Poles seen exporting sugar from surpluses.

text.p: The Czech Republic and Poland should both have sugar to export from their improved 1996/97 crops but tonnages have yet to be fixed due to unclear government policies, trade house E D & F Man said on Tuesday.

In Poland, eastern Europe's third largest beet producer, the surplus from the 1996/97 crop would increase with production now expected to reach 2.05 million tonnes white value, Man said in a monthly report. But the amount of sugar to be taken into stocks is still uncertain and only a small portion of the projected surplus has been earmarked for export subsidies.

"With the prospect of a 400,000 tonne export surplus but with only 118,300 tonnes of subsidised exports, the industry is trying to encourage the government to take sugar in its intervention stocks," Man said.
"The Agriculture Ministry has hinted recently it could absorb part of the remaining surplus by rebuilding state reserves but some of this sugar may still need to be exported."

In the Czech Republic, Man said the prospect of large-scale imports had convinced the government of the need to introduce import tariffs in spite of its earlier free-trade proclamations, but the improved beet crop had forced a change in thinking.

"Now it seems that the prospect of large-scale surpluses may be enticing the government to acknowledge the need to back a policy that could accommodate exports," it said. In its first estimate of the world 1996/97 sugar balance, issued in September, Man pegged Czech output at 543,000 tonnes raw value after a previous 462,000 tonnes.
Man said many east European nations had introduced tariffs to cushion domestic sugar prices from the vagaries of the world market price.

But as they were having problems coping with domestic supply surpluses, lack of investment and limited financing in agriculture, they were having to take further steps to support their domestic sugar industry.
